HIST 500: An examination of the theory and methodologies of the historical discipline and classic works of historiography.
HIST 510: The purpose of this course is to explore the place of the natural environment in the late medieval and early modern world.
HIST 511: Readings and research in major themes of the history of medieval Britain.
HIST 512: This course provides students with an overview of the political developments of church and secular government in medieval Europe.
HIST 513: This graduate seminar explores the major scholarly developments in the study of women's history, masculinity, and gendered representations in early modern Europe (1400-1800) and several colonial areas.
HIST 514: This course covers the basic historical information, historiographical orientation, and theoretical discussions of the major problems of global history between the end of the Middle Ages and the beginning of the modern world.
HIST 515: A graduate seminar examining selected topics in early modern European history through readings, discussions, and research papers.
HIST 516: A critical analysis of gender and theories of gender in selected American historical contexts.
HIST 522: The course examines the possible use of social theory by historians and explores how theory could inform historical writing.
HIST 523: Over 100 million people were victims of mass killings, including genocide, in the 20th century.
HIST 524: Historiography of deviance, crime, and madness in Europe from the late-18th century to the present.
HIST 525: This course provides students with an overview of the processes of constructing borders in a variety of forms, ethnic, religious, trade, and linguistic, in a European imperial context.
HIST 527: The social and cultural history of warefare in modern Europe, with specific emphasis on the First and Second World Wars.
HIST 530: This course exposes students to the current state of scholarship from the standpoint of historical, legal, sociological, and literary analyses of science in the early modern period.
HIST 531: This course is a research seminar covering the historiography of early modern Europe, the Ottoman Empire, Mughal India, Warring-State and early Tokugawa Japan, Choson Korea, and the history of Ming and Qing China with a focus on the interaction between religious and political history.
HIST 535: This course provides students with an overview of the contribution of intelectual and cultural historians to the field of "body history.
HIST 537: This seminar provides an overview of early modern Atlantic history from the late fifteenth to the early nineteenth centuries.
HIST 539: Studies in the history of wars and of the political, social, economic, diplomatic, and theoretical foundations of warfare.
HIST 540: Surveying Native American history from the pre-colonial era to the present, this course examines key historical events, including: Indigenous civilizations before colonialism; the invasion of North America by Europeans; colonial epidemics; the Indian slave trade; the Pueblo Revolt; the Seven Years' War; the development and impacts of U.S. Indian policy; Indigenous sovereignty.
HIST 541: The study of the causes, conduct, and political, social, diplomatic, cultural, and economic consequences of war from 1500 to the present.
HIST 542: This course provides graduate students with an introduction to the field of American borderlands studies.
HIST 543: Primarily a reading seminar, this course focuses on United States history from the 17th century to 1877, emphasizing the profound ways that the British American colonies and then the United States changed through numerous social, cultural, economic, and political revolutions.
HIST 544: Background and impact of the Civil War and the two succeeding decades, with emphasis on historiography and selected topics.
HIST 545: Primarily a reading seminar, this course focuses on United States history from 1877 to the present, emphasizing the profound ways the nation changed socially, culturally, economically, and politically since the late nineteenth century.
HIST 546: Readings and research in major themes of the history of the United States in the twentieth century.
HIST 547: Slavery in South America, the Caribbean, and North America from 16th century European colonization through the 19th century abolition movement.
HIST 548: This course offers a survey of American history from roughly the fifteenth to twentieth centuries.
HIST 551: This seminar provides students with an overview of important topics and debates related to the African American Freedom Struggle from Reconstruction to the present.
HIST 552: This course considers the political, cultural and social history of the United States from 1975 to the present.
HIST 553: This course offers a survey of the history of the place that became the United States through the lens of the environment.
HIST 556: Surveying Social and Cultural History in the 19th and 20th centuries in the United States, this course examines key themes and topics in the history of the field, including: race, class, gender, sexuality, labor, migration, citizenship, incarceration, and environment.
HIST 557: This course introduces graduate students to key historiographical and methodological literatures and debates in the field of modern Middle Eastern history.
HIST 558: This course provides a thorough grounding in the relationship between colonialism and nationalism in the Middle East, as well as in the emergence of modern nation-states and national identities.
HIST 559: This course investigates the history of mass movement within and out of the Middle East, the Balkans, and North Africa from the late nineteenth century to the present day.
HIST 561: This course offers an overview of the historiography of the Ottoman Empire.
HIST 562: The course provides an in-depth examination of key topics in recent research on the study of women, gender, and sexuality in the Middle East and an investigation of changes in the field.
HIST 563: This course provides an analysis of the modern Middle East in a global context.
HIST 564: The course provides an in-depth examination of key topics in recent research on the study of Islamic jurisprudence (fiqh) and theory (usul) and an investigation of changes in the field.
HIST 565: This course provides a thorough grounding in the state of the field of the history of Palestine/Israel.
HIST 567: Latin American colonial history was defined by exploitation for profit; the efficiency of state control over Indigenous and Afro-descendant populations established economic profit or loss.
HIST 568: This graduate course explores the history of medicine, science, and technology in early modern Latin America and Iberia, integrating interdisciplinary approaches and local/global contexts.
HIST 569: HIST 569 gives students an overview of key literatures, methodologies, and debates in the historiography of Latin America (the writing of Latin American history), from the 1490s to the Independence period (mostly, but by no means solely, the 1820s).
HIST 570: This seminar gives students an overview of central literatures and debates in the historiography of Latin America (the writing of Latin American history) and the Americas more broadly, from approximately to 1800 to the present.
HIST 571: HIST 571 gives students an overview of key literatures, methodologies, and debates in the historiography of Latin American ethnohistory, from the fifteenth to the nineteenth centuries.
HIST 572: From initial colonial contact, Latin America represents a site of violent conquest by European colonizers over indigenous populations and exploitation of both African and indigenous labor; white control over black and brown bodies was at the very core of colonial economic success or failure.
HIST 573: HIST 573 gives students an overview of key literatures, methodologies, and debates in the historiography of empire and society in Latin American history, fifteenth to nineteenth centuries.
HIST 579: This course focuses on East Asian religious history, starting with the formation of several major traditions in ancient China and ending with major religious trends in the modern era.
HIST 580: This course offers a foundation in early modern Asia from roughly the fifteenth to mid-nineteenth centuries.
HIST 581: Primarily a reading seminar, this course focuses on Chinese history from the Ming Dynasty (1368-1644) to the present, emphasizing the profound ways that the Ming Dynasty, Qing Dynasty, Republican China, and then the People's Republic of China changed through social, cultural, economic, and political transformations and revolutions.
HIST 582: Examines the historical literature on women and gender in late imperial and twentieth century China.
HIST 583: A research seminar, this course focuses on rebellion and revolution in Chinese history from the mid-nineteenth century to the present.
HIST 584: This course focuses on theoretical and applied medical knowledge as it developed in ancient China, spread to Japan and Korea, and developed over time to the modern era.
HIST 585: This course provides a thorough grounding in the state of the field of environmental history in Asia, including East Asia, Southeast Asia, and South Asia.
HIST 586: This course focuses on Japanese history from the early development of a state in the seventh century to the present.
HIST 587: Research and readings in the history of South Asia since the late eighteenth century.
HIST 588: A research seminar, this course examines Chinese history from a multi-ethnic perspective.
HIST 589: This course provides students with the thematic and theoretical foundation for the study and teaching of world history.
HIST 595: Supervised off-campus, nongroup instruction, including field experiences, practicums, or internships.
HIST 596: Creative projects, including nonthesis research, which are supervised on an individual basis and which fall outside the scope of formal courses.
HIST 597: Formal courses given on a topical or special interest subject which may be offered infrequently; several different topics may be taught in one year or term.
HIST 602: Students enrolled will lead discussion sections, grade papers and examinations, given an occasional lecture, and assist instructors in planning survey level courses.
HIST 603: Foreign study and/or research constituting progress toward the degree at a foreign university.
